subject: chemistry
title: Chemistry in Practice Investigation
level: Common brief for Higher and Ordinary level (same brief; the NCCA says it is assessed at the level you sit the written paper)
keyDates: January 2026 — SEC issued the live 2027 brief (ASTIR reports briefs for eight Tranche 1 subjects, including Chemistry, released in January 2026)
Friday 23 April 2027 — coursework must be completed and submitted to your class teacher (SEC brief, section 1); the school then submits to the SEC
Before 23 April 2027 — your school may set earlier internal deadlines for drafts, log check-ins and the final report; ask your teacher (not published by the SEC)
Date the SEC Schools Portal circular on PDF file naming and digital submission issues — TBC by SEC (circular issues each year)
June 2027 — written paper (300 marks, 60%); exact timetable date not checked here
summary: The Chemistry in Practice Investigation is a supervised piece of coursework worth 200 marks (40% of Leaving Cert Chemistry). For 2027 the brief asks you to investigate how the rate of a chemical reaction can be controlled: you research the chemistry, design and run a lab experiment under your teacher's supervision, analyse your own data, and write a digital report of no more than 1500 words that is submitted to the SEC as a PDF.

stages.name: Stage 1: Initial response to the brief
stages.marksNote: Feeds A (50): title, introduction, research question, hypothesis; and D (50): relevance and coherence from the start.

points: The 2027 brief is on controlling the rate of chemical reactions. It lists reaction types (acid-base, decomposition, redox, combination, displacement, precipitation) and rate factors (concentration, surface area, temperature, pressure, catalyst).
It says effects can be measured directly or indirectly, depending on the chemical and physical changes involved, so you have freedom to choose your own method.
It links the topic to health, sustainability and technology (for example pharmaceuticals and battery technology). You will be marked for relating your work to real-world issues, so note a link early.
The instruction is 'investigate one or more aspects of this topic'. The SEC brief does not say you must pick exactly one reaction and one factor, but doing so keeps a 1500-word report focused.

The SEC says the investigation should follow the six NCCA stages: initial response, background research, design and planning, conducting the experiment, data analysis and conclusions, and finalising the report.

The NCCA suggests asking: What do I already know? What do I need to find out? Which experiment am I interested in? Could I adapt an experiment I have already done, or develop an original one? What sources will I use and how will I record them?
Connect your idea to your own interests and to experiments and theory you have already met in class, such as collision theory and the rates-of-reaction practicals.
Check feasibility early with your teacher: equipment, chemicals, time and safety. The NCCA says discussing limitations and how to overcome them is part of this stage.
Your idea must be your own. If classmates choose the same reaction and factor, your projects still cannot be identical.
The log is your working document: ideas, sources with download dates, calculations, photos, problems and decisions. It can be digital or paper and its format is your choice.
It is not submitted to the SEC, but the NCCA advises sharing it with your teacher regularly because it supports authentication of your work.
Record the reasons for key decisions as you make them. You will draw on this when writing the report.

checklistCandidates: Read the SEC brief fully and note the health, sustainability or technology link you could use
Pick a reaction and a rate factor that your school lab can safely handle
Start an investigative log and add to it at every stage
Check your idea's feasibility and safety with your teacher before committing

stages.name: Stage 2: Background research
stages.marksNote: Feeds A (50): background research (secondary data), evaluation of secondary data, referencing; also D: relevance, coherence.

points: Research the chemistry behind your investigation: the reaction, its equation, the rate factor and why it should affect rate (for example collision theory and activation energy).
The NCCA says research should be broader than the experiment: wider scientific context, socio-scientific implications and media arguments linked to the brief.
Use a range of sources and compare viewpoints. Good practice is to review, summarise and evaluate evidence rather than list it.
Develop a research question on a specific issue from the brief, informed by this research.
The top descriptor requires you to evaluate a wide range of appropriate sources, not just quote them. Say briefly how reliable or useful each is.
Explain ideas in your own words. Pasted text without proper acknowledgement is plagiarism, which the SEC treats as cheating.
Show how the research shaped your experiment, for example why you chose a method, a concentration range or a measurement technique.
Reference inside the text and in a reference list. The reference list does not count towards the 1500 words.
The NCCA does not require a particular style, but each reference needs enough detail for a reader to verify it: author, title, year and page for print; hyperlink and date accessed for online sources.
Any AI-generated material must be acknowledged: name the tool, the date, and how you used it. Include the shareable chat URL if the tool gives one, or the tool name and the prompt if it does not.
The SEC brief points to Appendices 1 and 2 of the SEC Coursework Rules and Procedures for its referencing and AI requirements. Read these yourself.
Record extracts, secondary data, your own reflections, download dates and references in your log as you go. Chasing sources the night before submission is a common way to lose referencing marks.

checklistCandidates: Write a focused research question based on your background research
Explain the relevant chemistry in your own words with correct terms and equations
Evaluate how reliable and useful each source is, not just list them
Reference every source in the text and in the list, including any AI use
Say how your research influenced your experimental design

stages.name: Stage 3: Designing and planning the experiment
stages.marksNote: Feeds A (50): hypothesis; B (50): experimental design, method, safety, fairness, accuracy, selection of equipment.

points: State a testable hypothesis based on chemical theory, and explain briefly why you expect that result. The top descriptor wants a hypothesis underpinned by chemical concepts, not a guess.
You can design an original experiment or extend or adapt one you have already done in class.
Plan to collect quantitative primary data. Decide whether you will measure rate directly or indirectly, as the brief allows.
Identify your independent variable (what you change), dependent variable (what you measure) and controlled variables (what you keep constant), with values where possible.
Explain how the test is fair: what you control and how. Plan repeat trials and say why they improve reliability.
Choose equipment to suit the precision you need, and justify the choice. Selection of equipment is a named marking criterion.
Consider validity, accuracy, precision, error and integrity, as the NCCA lists them. State assumptions and decisions and how they affect the results.
Plan the quantities and concentrations of chemicals and how you will prepare them.
Identify specific hazards and the precaution for each. Safety is a named marking criterion.
Safety, GDPR and access to property are listed by the NCCA as mandatory requirements you must follow.
The NCCA says it is good practice to have used your chosen apparatus in class first, so you understand its limits. Record any compromises you make because of equipment.
Your teacher can discuss feasibility with you and should step in only if your design is likely to be unsafe. The design must be yours.
The SEC says brevity is rewarded but unwarranted length loses coherence marks. Give a clear method with the reason for each decision, without padding.

checklistCandidates: State a testable hypothesis with a chemical-theory reason
Name the independent, dependent and controlled variables
Plan repeat trials and say how they improve reliability
Justify your choice of equipment for the precision needed
List each hazard with a specific precaution
Get your teacher's sign-off on safety before starting

stages.name: Stage 4: Conducting the experiment
stages.marksNote: Feeds B (50): method, accuracy, fairness; C (50): experimental observations (primary data).

points: The SEC requires the experiment and the gathering of primary data to be fully completed under the direct supervision of your Chemistry teacher, in a safe, relevant setting such as the school lab.
Each student carries out their own experiment. Classmates may help you handle equipment, but the investigation remains your own work.
A typical experiment takes about 1-2 hours of lab time. Because of lab capacity you may have several sessions, so plan other work (analysis, research) for when you are not in the lab.

Your teacher is present at all times. The NCCA says they should not intervene if you use equipment incorrectly but safely, record observations poorly or make errors. These are part of what you report on honestly.
Record all observations and data, qualitative and quantitative, in your log as you work.
Photograph your apparatus set-up and your results where useful. Remember the 20-image limit in the report.
Record unanticipated outcomes and anomalies. The NCCA says unexpected outcomes are a valid part of science and should be reflected on, and you do not need the result you predicted.
Use correct units and repeat trials as planned. Note any change from your plan and the reason.
The teacher must be able to confirm that the experiment you ran matches the research and plan you shared with them. Share your plan before the lab session.

checklistCandidates: Run the experiment only under your teacher's direct supervision
Record observations as well as numbers, with units
Photograph the apparatus and results for possible use in the report
Note anomalies, difficulties and any changes to your plan
Repeat trials as planned

stages.name: Stage 5: Data analysis and conclusions
stages.marksNote: Feeds C (50): data presentation, data analysis, conclusions; and D (50): reflective approach.

points: Present data in clear tables with units and repeated trials, and calculate averages correctly.
Use graphs or calculations to find patterns and relationships. Label axes with quantities and units.
Judge your data for accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility, and identify and explain any anomalous results.
Describe the pattern in words, then explain it using chemistry theory. Saying 'it increased' without a reason does not reach the top descriptor.
Answer your research question directly and state whether the data support your hypothesis. Base this on what the data show, not on what you expected.
Link the conclusion back to the hypothesis and the research question you set.

Evaluate your investigation: reliability, sources of error and limitations in the research, the design and the data gathering. The top descriptor requires acknowledging limitations in all three areas.
Suggest practical, specific improvements, and optionally extensions.
Share your analysis with your teacher. They must be satisfied that your analysis and conclusions are aligned with the experiments done under their supervision.

checklistCandidates: Present results in labelled tables and graphs with units
Calculate means correctly and show your working
Explain each pattern with chemistry theory, not just describe it
State whether the data supports your hypothesis
Identify errors and limitations in research, design and data gathering
Suggest specific improvements

stages.name: Stage 6: Finalising and submitting the report
stages.marksNote: Feeds all of A-D; D (50) is judged across the whole report: communication, coherence, relevance, reflective approach.

points: Download the SEC cover page (Word format) and make it the first page of your document. The SEC does not provide a template.
Maximum 1500 words. The count excludes references, data tables, formulae or equations, and labels. Going over may lose marks.

Maximum 20 images, treated as a limit not a target. No videos. Do not use images to carry extra text. Avoid images where people can be identified. Formulae and equations do not count towards the image limit.
Use the seven headings in order: 1 Title and Introduction, 2 Background Research, 3 Designing and Planning, 4 Conducting the Experiment, 5 Data and Data Analysis, 6 Conclusions, 7 References.

Formatting: numbered headings, each starting on a new page, Arial 14 bold black; body text Arial 12, black, 1.5 line spacing; bold, italics, numbering and bullets allowed; no coloured or highlighted text; portrait only; page numbers bottom-centre; 20 mm margins and nothing in the margins.
Graphs, diagrams and images can be made with software, taken from sources (with a reference), photographed or hand-drawn. Photograph or scan handwritten equations.
Use your log to write an authentic account of what you did, including difficulties and what you changed.
Keep it consistent: points from your research and design should come back in your analysis and conclusion.

Link to real-world applications in health, sustainability or technology, as the brief does, and say how your outcome fits broader scientific or societal issues. The top descriptor on the work of scientists in society needs a considered reflection.
Your teacher can give general, non-directive feedback only. They must not edit your draft or supply model text, and the NCCA says they should not correct the report for redrafting.
The SEC says short, clear writing earns credit, and length that makes the report incoherent loses credit.
Convert to PDF. Print the PDF and proof-read it. Anything not visible on the printout will not be visible to examiners and cannot earn marks.
Give the digital file to your class teacher by Friday 23 April 2027. File naming is set by an SEC Schools Portal circular, so ask your teacher.
Sign the SEC Authentication Form P.2, which your teacher and school principal also sign. The school keeps a printed and digital copy until appeals end, and submits through the Schools Portal.
Keep your own backup copy of the report as you work.

checklistCandidates: Put the SEC cover page first
Use the seven SEC headings in order, each on a new page
Keep to 1500 words and no more than 20 images
Format in Arial, black, 14 bold headings, 12 body, 1.5 spacing, 20 mm margins
Link results to health, sustainability or technology
Reference every source and any AI use
Convert to PDF, print and proof-read it
Sign the P.2 authentication form and hand in by 23 April 2027

criteria.name: A: Title and Introduction, Background Research, References
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: You clearly understand the task and explain what you are investigating and why; you pose a probing research question and a testable hypothesis based on chemical concepts; you use relevant research from a wide range of appropriate sources and evaluate them; you explain the chemistry clearly and accurately; you reference properly.

criteria.name: B: Designing and Planning, Conducting the Experiment
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: You use a thorough investigative design and appropriate methods to collect high-quality primary data. The SEC lists experimental design, method, safety, fairness, accuracy and selection of equipment.

criteria.name: C: Data and Data Analysis, Conclusions
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: You present clear, appropriate data and analysis; draw valid conclusions justified by the data and related to your hypotheses; and thoroughly evaluate the investigation, acknowledging limitations in research, design and data gathering.

criteria.name: D: Scientific Literacy (judged across the whole report)
criteria.whatTopMarksLook: The SEC lists communication, coherence, relevance and reflective approach. The NCCA top descriptor asks for a coherent, consistent report with references and reflections, and a considered reflection placing your results in broader societal and scientific issues relating to the brief.

rules: Work must be entirely your own and individual. Each student submits their own report, even if classmates investigate the same thing.
Experiment and primary data collection must be done under the direct supervision of your Chemistry teacher in a safe setting.

Reference all sources, including any AI use (tool name, date, how used, and the shareable URL or the prompt). Unreferenced material is plagiarism, treated as cheating and investigated by the SEC under Section 18 of its Coursework Rules; penalties can include withholding results.
The SEC Coursework Rules and Procedures apply in full, and you, your teacher and the school authority share responsibility for authenticity.
Use the SEC cover page as the first page, convert the report to PDF, print and proof-read it, and sign Authentication Form P.2 (teacher and principal also sign).
Maximum 1500 words (excluding references, data tables, formulae/equations and labels) and 20 images; no videos; images must not carry extra text.
Follow the formatting rules: Arial, black text only, 14 bold numbered headings on new pages, 12 body text at 1.5 spacing, portrait, 20 mm margins, page numbers bottom-centre.
The investigative log is not submitted to the SEC.
Teachers may not edit drafts, give model text or design your investigation for you; feedback must be general and non-directive.
Hand in to your teacher by Friday 23 April 2027, or any earlier school deadline.
mistakes: Ignoring formatting rules (wrong font, spacing, margins) or going over the word count (Institute of Education masterclass).
Using images to carry text instead of explanation.
Weak or unclear conclusions, or conclusions that do not link back to the hypothesis.
Graphs and tables without labels or units.
No reflection on results, errors or improvements.
Describing a trend without explaining it with chemistry theory (Studyclix guide).
Copying or paraphrasing sources without referencing them, or leaving out AI acknowledgements.
Padding the report so it loses coherence; the SEC explicitly penalises unwarranted length.
Leaving work in the margins or not proof-reading the printed PDF, so content is not visible to examiners.
Not showing how the research influenced the design, or not coming back to earlier points in the analysis and conclusion.
Submitting work too similar to a classmate who chose the same experiment.

conflicts: Level: the app says the investigation is 'taken at a common level'. The SEC brief is headed 'Higher Level and Ordinary Level' and the NCCA says it uses a common brief and is assessed at the level at which you sit the written paper. 'Common brief' is the more accurate wording.

Brief timing: the app says the brief is published in term 2 of Year 1. That matches the NCCA guidelines, and for the 2027 cohort the live brief was issued in January 2026 (ASTIR). No conflict, but the app could say it has already been issued.

Marks and submission details missing from the app: it does not give 200 marks, the 23 April 2027 completion date, the 1500-word and 20-image limits, the seven headings or the formatting rules. These come from the official SEC brief and should be added.

Marks by criteria: the app's four areas follow the NCCA descriptor rows (knowledge; design and method; analysis and conclusions; work of scientists in society). The SEC mark allocation uses four 50-mark blocks with different labels (A title/introduction/research/references, B designing and conducting, C data analysis and conclusions, D scientific literacy). Both are official; use the SEC split for marks and the NCCA rows for what the top band looks like. The SEC brief does not publish band-by-band mark ranges.

Hours: the app says 'up to 20 hours'. The NCCA says approximately 20 hours in total, while its stage estimates (1-2, 2-3, 2-3, 1-2, 1-2, up to 4) add up to roughly 11-16 hours. These are guides, not limits.

Studyclix wording differs from the SEC brief: Studyclix's reproduction tells students to choose one reaction and one factor and lists required steps. The official SEC brief says 'investigate one or more aspects of this topic'. I trust the SEC brief. Studyclix also gives about 300 words per section and 3-4 hours per section; these are its own estimates, not SEC rules (the SEC sets only the 1500-word total).
Other subjects' dates differ: the Biology brief's date is 26 February 2027, not 23 April. The 23 April date is for Chemistry only, per the Chemistry SEC brief.

The Institute of Education deck says a digital and printed copy of the PDF are submitted. The SEC brief says the student gives the digital file to the teacher, the school keeps the printed and digital copies, and the school submits through the Schools Portal. I follow the SEC brief.
